source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC6559129 (abstract, all sections to Conclusions, reference list for refs 10, 44, 45, 62, 77), read in my own browser tab and saved to my folder; Fig. 1 is a process flowchart with no claim numbers

claims.note: Correctly labelled second-hand: the review cites Hargrove et al. 2018 (ref 45; Slavova is a co-author of both). The percentages are the prevalence of gabapentin among overdose decedents in 2013 (2.9%) and 2014 (17%); routine testing began in July 2014, so the 2014 figure includes months before it. The claim could give the two years. 'Raised' follows the review's own causal wording ('resulted in'); no other explanation is examined. The review also supports 'what is tested changes what is found' and 'access to testing differs' more generally: no national postmortem toxicology standard, many offices do not test all suspected overdoses for new substances including fentanyl, and the one region not testing every case for gabapentin had the lowest prevalence.

anchors.locator: Epidemiologic Analysis of Drug Overdose Death Data > Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Abrupt changes can come from new toxicology panels: routine gabapentin testing introduced in Kentucky in July 2014 raised the prevalence of gabapentin among overdose decedents from 2.9% (2013) to 17% (2014), citing Hargrove et al. 2018; the authors note that gradual procedural improvements produce smaller, harder-to-detect changes.

anchors.locator: Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Lack of routine testing for some analytes changes how often substances are detected and hinders comparisons between jurisdictions; in a multi-jurisdiction gabapentin study the region with the lowest prevalence was the only one not testing every potential overdose for gabapentin; the authors call for reporting the type of testing (screening or confirmatory, routine or on request).

anchors.locator: Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths > The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: The US has no nationally accepted standards for postmortem toxicology; many offices do not test all suspected overdoses for new psychoactive substances including fentanyl and analogues; a National Forensic Laboratory Information System survey estimates only 75% of offices always request testing for opioids other than heroin or fentanyl, and 51%-75% always request testing for fentanyl and heroin.

claims.note: All four South Carolina numbers confirmed (rate ratio 1.98). The rate is age-adjusted T40.2-T40.4, which includes T40.4 (synthetic opioids, including illicitly made fentanyl); the review elsewhere says illicit fentanyl reached Southern states in 2013-2014, and its 'primarily' (the claim's 'mainly') is the authors' judgment, resting on a personal communication from the state's vital statistics office for the 2014 procedural change, not on a decomposition. Other passages bear on the claim: text search cannot help the roughly 20% of overdose certificates naming no drug; the review reports Ruhm's 2015 adjustment as 21% above the reported rate (12.46 vs 10.31 per 100,000, matching the claim's 33,091 to 39,999, ratio 1.209) and Buchanich's about 70,000 deaths, and judges both assumptions reasonable but difficult to verify (Buchanich is a co-author of this review). A Kentucky study it cites found cocaine listed as a contributing drug on 77% of certificates and alprazolam on 67% (denominators not stated in the review); this is listing when detected, not a miss rate, so the claim's 'no study read here measured how often stimulants ... are missed' stands, but the editors may wish to note it.

anchors.locator: Epidemiologic Analysis of Drug Overdose Death Data > Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: South Carolina's age-adjusted prescription-opioid poisoning rate (T40.2-T40.4) went from 4.7/100,000 (2013) to 9.3/100,000 (2014) (CDC WONDER); the authors say this mainly reflected the rise in drug-poisoning certificates listing specific drugs from 57.7% to 94.4%, after the state vital statistics office began collecting specific drug names in January 2014 (personal correspondence), not a real worsening.

anchors.locator: Identifying Specific Opioids by Cause-of-Death Text Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: ICD-10 data cannot identify most specific opioids; literal-text search helps, but cannot be applied to the roughly 20% of US overdose certificates that name no specific drug, so it does not fix the undercount of opioid involvement.

anchors.locator: Statistical Adjustment for Undercounting, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Buchanich et al. reallocated unspecified unintentional overdose deaths by state and year in proportion to specified deaths: about 70,000 opioid deaths possibly uncounted in 1999-2015. Ruhm's model put the 2015 opioid-involved rate at 12.46 against a reported 10.31 per 100,000 (21% higher). The review calls both assumptions reasonable but difficult to verify, and says data on jurisdiction type and testing protocols that could improve such models are not readily available.

anchors.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 1st paragraph; Death Certificate ICD-10 Coding, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Counts for specific drugs are only as accurate as the drugs listed on certificates; omissions from a certifier's practice or office policy can severely bias rates. A record whose only drug code is T50.9 typically means no drug name or class was written.

anchors.locator: Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Kentucky study (cited): benzodiazepines were less often listed as contributing drugs on certificates (alprazolam 67%, clonazepam and diazepam under 40%) than fentanyl (89%), heroin (88%), methadone (81%) or cocaine (77%); the denominator is not stated in the review.

anchors.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Provisional data undercount overdose deaths while investigations are pending (R99 used as underlying cause until completion); the R99 share varies inversely with deaths coded as drug poisoning.

anchors.locator: Death Certificates Remain the Core of Population-Based Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Citing Hedegaard et al., the share of overdose certificates identifying specific drugs or classes rose every year from 75% (2011) to 85% (2016), which may influence drug-specific trends.

claims.overstatement: The figures are in the review, but 'Maryland, a central medical-examiner state' is not: the review names no state's system type here and attributes the variation to office policies that do not follow professional recommendations, not to the type of official. Outside this source (editors to confirm): Connecticut and Massachusetts also have statewide medical examiner offices, so 68% against 1% is a contrast among central medical-examiner states. Placed in a list of coroner-versus-medical-examiner findings, it can be read as an ME/coroner difference. Also 'drug poisoning deaths', not 'poisoning deaths'.
claims.note: Confirmed: as of 2016, undetermined intent ranged from 1% (Connecticut, Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland) of drug poisoning deaths (CDC WONDER, ref 44), correctly labelled 'as cited'. The same paragraph cites Warner et al. 2013: Maryland 85%, Utah over 40%, national average 8%. The review also gives Warner's four system averages for certificates listing drugs (centralized ME 92%, decentralized ME 71%, hybrid 73%, coroner 62%), the same figures the claim takes from Slavova 2015 with the middle two left out. It says that ME and coroner selection (appointed or elected) and credentialing vary, and that jurisdiction-type data are not readily available for modelling.

anchors.locator: Epidemiologic Analysis of Drug Overdose Death Data > Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Jurisdictions vary in classing drug poisoning deaths as undetermined rather than unintentional or suicide, which affects comparisons by intent. Warner et al.: Maryland 85%, Utah over 40%, national 8% undetermined. NAME recommends 'accident' for opioid misuse deaths without apparent self-harm intent. As of 2016, undetermined still ranged from 1% (Connecticut and Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland); the authors suggest office policies not aligned with professional recommendations may drive this.

anchors.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Citing Warner et al.: states with centralized medical examiner systems averaged 92% of overdose certificates listing drugs, against decentralized systems: medical examiner 71%, hybrid 73%, coroner 62%.

anchors.locator: Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths > The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Death investigations are run by medical examiners and/or coroners, who vary in how they are selected (appointed or elected) and in professional credentials.
Jurisdiction characteristics such as ME/coroner type and testing protocols could improve adjustment models but are not readily available.
